food.text: The same Arctic Small Tool tradition groups also camped along inland streams to catch salmon, giving them a second major food source beyond the coast. Some of these camps were temporary, while others included more permanent, sod-roofed homes.

At a coastal site on Magnetic Island, on Alaska's Cook Inlet, archaeologists uncovered hearths and fire-cracked cooking stones dated to about 1800 to 1400 BCE. Stone tools found alongside them were linked to the Arctic Small Tool tradition.

Archaeological excavations show that larger, barren-ground-sized caribou first appeared in western Greenland about 4,000 years ago. Caribou like these became a vital source of food, clothing and shelter for Arctic peoples from prehistoric times onward.
Many researchers believe it was Arctic Small Tool tradition people who first introduced the bow and arrow to the Arctic. This technology eventually became part of later Eskimo archery culture.

Arctic Small Tool tradition hunters made composite arrows and spears fitted with small stone blades, using shafts of bone or antler. Their camps, often along coasts and streams, let them take advantage of seal or salmon populations.

art.text: At Alta in northern Norway, hunter-gatherers carved more than 6,000 rock images of reindeer, boats, and bears over many centuries. Their art reveals a culture skilled at reindeer herding, boat building, and shamanistic ritual, including a bear cult reflected in many carvings.

A paleo-Eskimo carving called First Face, made from walrus ivory in the shape of an abstract human face, is between 3,900 and 3,600 years old. Found on Devon Island, it is one of the oldest known depictions of a human face created in North America.

In southern Peary Land, north of Independence Fjord, the Independence I people built dwellings with an elliptical floor plan using tools made from rock and bone. They hunted musk oxen and Arctic hares, with musk-ox bones showing the area was inhabited by 2000 BC and the oldest finds dated to 2400 BC.

At Alta, bears appear so often in the rock carvings, and in poses that suggest reverence rather than only hunting, that researchers see an active bear cult among the carvers. This devotion to bears sits alongside the same carvers' images of reindeer herds and boats.

The Independence I people occupied one of the most extreme environments in the Arctic, and their dwellings were designed with a focus on keeping warm in response to this harsh topography. Radiocarbon dating shows their dwellings and tools changed little in style throughout the culture's long existence.

The depiction of bears in the Alta carvings seems to have ceased around 1700 BC, which might indicate a change in religious beliefs around that time. Bears had earlier been shown with tracks coming out of their dens, which led some researchers to speculate that bears were connected with a cult of the afterlife, or of death in general.

Independence I dwellings dated after about 1800 BC are found mostly south of Independence Fjord, continuing until around 1300 BC, while earlier dwellings dating back to about 2400 BC lay further north. It remains unknown whether the builders moved south or the culture simply came to an end where it stood.

In the Alta carvings, tracks coming out of bear dens are often shown running vertically through the image and crossing the horizontal tracks of other animals. Some researchers speculate this shows bears were connected with a cult of the afterlife or of death in general, since the vertical tracks seem to indicate an ability of bears to pass between different layers of the world.

science.text: In February 2010, scientists reported the first genome sequencing of an ancient human. The man was found in Greenland and is believed to be from the prehistoric Saqqaq culture.

Paleo-Eskimos spread rapidly from Alaska as far as Greenland and Labrador, and their use of the bow and arrow may have helped. They are credited with introducing this technology to populations in Eastern Canada by 2000 BCE.

The genome of the Greenland man suggested a distinct migration of peoples from Siberia to North America some 5,500 years ago. It was independent of earlier migrations, and by 4,500 years ago descendants of this migration had reached Greenland.

The genome came from fragments of hair 4,000 years old. The National Museum of Denmark, the Beijing Genomics Institute and other collaborating scientific institutions sequenced nearly 80% of the Paleo-Eskimo man's genome.

The earliest inhabitants of North America's central and eastern Arctic are called the Arctic small tool tradition, which existed around 2500 BCE. It consisted of several Paleo-Eskimo cultures, including the Independence cultures and Pre-Dorset cultures.

Paleo-Eskimo archaeological cultures are grouped under the Arctic Small Tool tradition, which includes the Saqqaq, Independence, Pre-Dorset and Dorset cultures in the Canadian Arctic and Greenland. Its source has been argued to lie in the Syalakh-Bel'kachi-Ymyyakhtakh culture sequence of East Siberia.
The Saqqaq culture of Greenland is dated to 2500 to 800 BCE. The Independence I culture of northeastern Canada and Greenland dates to about 2400 to 1800 BCE.

The Saqqaq people arrived in western Greenland from Arctic Canada, and their sites include Sisimiut, inhabited for about 4,500 years. At that time the shoreline was up to several dozen meters above today's line. It gradually dropped over time because of post-glacial rebound.

Genetic comparisons indicate gene flow between the ancestors of the Dorset and of the Thule at least 4000 years ago, long before the Thule left the Bering Strait region. Later genetic data show no recent Dorset admixture, so the Thule replaced the Dorset with little or no interbreeding.

culture.text: The Saqqaq culture of southern Greenland lasted from around 2500 BCE until about 800 BCE. It was the earliest known culture in southern Greenland and the longest-residing culture in all of Greenland's history. It is named after the settlement of Saqqaq, the site of many archaeological finds.

Greenland had no human inhabitants until remarkably late, because its position made it hard to reach. With traditional transport, people could get there only through High Arctic Canada or by crossing the Nares Strait, one of the most extreme environments. Archaeologists estimate the first migration happened around 2500 BC.

Arctic Small Tool tradition camps are often found along coasts and streams, where people could take advantage of seal or salmon populations. Some groups were fairly nomadic, but more permanent sod-roofed homes have also been identified at their sites. The tradition developed around 2500 BC and its groups were the first human occupants of Arctic Canada and Greenland.

Independence I people lived in northern Greenland and the Canadian Arctic between 2400 and 1900 BC. The area was extremely harsh, so their dwellings focused on keeping warm. The culture is named after Independence Fjord in Peary Land.

Frozen remains of a Saqqaq man dubbed "Inuk" were found on Disko Island in western Greenland, at Qeqertarsuaq. He had brown eyes, black hair and shovel-shaped incisors, and lived about 4000 years ago. His DNA has been sequenced and shows he was related to indigenous populations in northeastern Siberia.

Arctic Small Tool tradition people used a distinctive toolkit based on microblade technology. Typical tools included scrapers, burins, and side and end blades. The blades were set into composite arrows or spears made of other materials, such as bone or antler.

The Independence I culture disappeared around 1900 to 1700 BC for unknown reasons, though the extreme temperatures of northern Greenland and the unreliability of muskox, their main food source and an animal prone to overhunting, could have contributed to its demise. Scholars still debate how the culture emerged and flourished in isolated northeastern Greenland, and when it vanished. Independence II, which followed, began in the 8th century BC, roughly 600 years later.

The Saqqaq culture came in two phases, and the main difference was that the newer phase adopted the use of sandstone. The younger phase of the Saqqaq culture coincides with the oldest phase of the Dorset culture.

The Saqqaq are not the ancestors of contemporary Kalaallit, the West Greenland Inuit. Their closest relatives are the modern Chukchis and Koryaks. It is not known whether they crossed into North America in boats or over ice.
